name: Carla Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers or government. This is confidential. Tell me about a usual working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at the shovel before daylight, check the bucket teeth, and take the radio from the previous operator. I like a clean handover and a road that the crew has actually inspected. My vocational course taught the basics, but most of my judgment came from years on the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that a faster form is fine, but the rock face and the haul road still decide our day. I don't use AI tools, and I wouldn't start just to save a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable with the work we know. Our wages cover the mortgage and we have a proper reserve, though I still check the grocery bill every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on operating the shovel and use the same paper fault log through the first year. I'd keep our regular mortgage payment and leave the children's music lessons in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. The shift has its ordinary hazards, but this picture doesn't put our income in doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the paper log help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mark the time when a bucket tooth loosens and hand the sheet to maintenance. A screen would have to beat that handover before I'd trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who looks after the money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ivo and I sit down with the bills on Sunday evening. We don't buy equipment or subscriptions we haven't needed.

say: I'd say **faster forms** could help, while rock and haul roads still determine how the shift goes.
I'd tell colleagues I see no reason to **change tools** merely to save a few minutes.
think: Our **mortgage** is covered and savings exceed six months, so this picture leaves me comfortable at work.
I still watch **grocery costs** because a strong reserve doesn't make the family budget careless.
do: Keep operating the **shovel** and hand maintenance the paper fault log throughout the first year.
Maintain our regular **mortgage payment** and the children's music lessons without changing the household budget.
feel: Fairly **calm** about work and money, though the shift still has its usual hazards.
S0.quote: I don't use AI tools, and I wouldn't start just to save a few minutes.
fieldNote: She has a working **paper handover** and sees no personal gain from replacing it merely for a small time saving.
Her strong **reserve** supports a calm mood, while a Sunday budget habit reflects care for family obligations.

steps.text: Operate the shovel and keep handing maintenance the paper fault log

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use software for orders and rosters, but people in the pit must be told when routes change. I don't want a machine deciding the haul road on a map it hasn't driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners might lose posts, and that would be hard for their families. My own seat looks safe while robots arrive slowly, but I fear a rushed trial could make the shift less safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety representative to put any new route plan through the normal site meeting. In the first year I'd keep a written list of wrong turns or missed closures and show it at that meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened for my wage. I feel protective of the crew when a neat plan reaches a muddy road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me one closure a planner could miss.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last rain, the south cut filled with water before the morning map changed. I stopped the shovel traffic until the supervisor saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the planning software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the mine trains us and shows that it catches closures faster than our radio calls. I won't volunteer our crew as a blind test.

say: I'd tell the **office** that faster ordering and rosters still need clear instructions for workers in the pit.
I'd insist that **route plans** face a safety meeting before changing where haul traffic goes.
think: I expect some **planning posts** could shrink, though my own shovel shifts look safe while robots spread slowly.
I fear a rushed **trial** could miss a muddy closure and put crew members in danger.
do: Ask the **safety representative** to bring each new route plan to the normal site meeting.
Keep a **written list** of missed closures in the first year and present it at the meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about crew safety and planners' jobs, while expecting my operator pay to continue.
S1.quote: I won't volunteer our crew as a blind test.
fieldNote: Her resistance is tied to a remembered **flooded cut**, so she asks for the established safety meeting rather than an abstract ban.
She is concerned for **planners** but expects her own income to hold while hands-on automation moves more slowly.

steps.text: Ask safety representative to review route plans at the site meeting
Record missed closures and present them at the site meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 could change the forms and dispatch calls, but 2031 is the date when robots might match our hands. Three years is a short apprenticeship for any machine that has to read rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay may hold at first, yet a robot shovel in 2031 could take away a whole set of shifts. We have savings and several mines nearby, but I cannot send the children to school on a promise of another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager this winter for the actual purchase timetable and write down what operators can still inspect. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply to nearby mines if our operator roster starts shrinking, and we'd defer replacing our car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wages if the roster begins to thin. I can make a few moves, but the family cannot absorb a permanent drop in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could the family live on savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little over eight months at our current spending, according to our Sunday ledger. I don't want to burn that while the mortgage keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivo about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Ivo that the old car stays until we see a secure roster. The children can still get to school in it.

say: I'd separate **2028** paperwork and dispatch changes from possible robot shovel work around **2031**.
I'd ask for a real **purchase timetable** before anyone tells operators their work will disappear.
think: My wage could hold at first, but a **robot shovel** around 2031 might remove many operator shifts.
Eight months of **savings** and nearby mines offer options, though the mortgage and school costs keep the risk serious.
do: Ask management for the **purchase timetable** this winter and list inspections operators still perform.
Apply to **nearby mines** if our roster shrinks after 2028, and defer buying a replacement car.
feel: **Anxious** about losing a large share of pay, with savings and nearby jobs giving some control.
S2.quote: I cannot send the children to school on a promise of another job.
fieldNote: Her **family obligations** make a hypothetical nearby vacancy feel less secure than a paid roster in hand.
She understands the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and hands-on robots, and makes applications conditional on reduced shifts.

steps.text: Apply to nearby mines if operator shifts shrink after 2028
Defer buying a replacement family car until the roster is secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 still changes dispatch and reports first, while robots may challenge shovel operators around 2034. I want a date on any proposed machine trial, not rumours by the lockers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets us reduce the mortgage before the hardest change. I still dislike betting on an unfamiliar control room, and I may be 51 when the robots arrive, with years of work left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shovel and put one extra mortgage payment in each year while the overtime lasts. If management announces a 2034 robot trial, I'd inspect the job board at nearby mines before choosing a training course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now, but I could become anxious if an actual trial takes shifts. The extra years give us a way to lower what the household needs each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay the mortgage instead of buying a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course with no promised place can eat money the bank will certainly take. One less mortgage payment later is a real gain for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would persuade you to take a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named job, paid training hours and proof that a person has done it safely for a year. I don't need to be first through that door.

say: I'd say **2031** changes reports first, with possible robot shovel competition around **2034**.
I'd ask management for a dated **trial notice** before treating locker-room rumours as a plan.
think: I can lower our **mortgage** over five years, but an unfamiliar control room feels like a risky wager.
I'd still have **working years** ahead in 2034, so losing operator shifts would matter even with savings.
do: Keep operating the **shovel** and make one extra mortgage payment each year while overtime lasts.
Check **nearby mine vacancies** if a robot trial is announced before choosing any course.
feel: **Uneasy** now; an actual trial that removes shifts could make the household risk sharper.
S3.quote: A course with no promised place can eat money the bank will certainly take.
fieldNote: She prefers a **certain mortgage reduction** to speculative training, matching her cautious approach to technology.
Her vacancy search is **conditional** on an announced trial; she does not claim to be retraining yet.

steps.text: Keep shovel shifts and watch for a dated robot trial notice
Make one extra mortgage payment each year while overtime lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 may change paperwork, and 2039 is the possible robot date for the shovel. Ten years is enough time to decide whether I want to end my working years on that machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when hands-on robots appear. Our children should be grown then, but I won't assume their needs or our mortgage vanish on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my operator certificate current and ask the mine about retirement terms in writing this year. I'd continue the extra mortgage payment when overtime permits, then decide nearer 2036 whether to take a shorter roster if one is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan, though I don't like anyone making a calendar for my last shift. The decade gives our family room to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a shorter roster workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage would need to be nearly cleared and the pension figures would need to add up. I wouldn't trade wages for a vague promise of time off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to change plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my partner Ivo and I want them to finish school without carrying our work worries. We can discuss their next steps when the time comes.

say: I'd distinguish **2036** paperwork changes from possible robot shovel work around **2039**.
I'd say a **decade** gives experienced operators room to make their own plans for later working years.
think: At **53 and 56**, I may want fewer shifts, but I cannot assume the mortgage or family costs disappear.
I'd need written **pension figures** before treating a shorter roster as affordable.
do: Keep my **operator certificate** current and request written retirement terms from the mine this year.
Make an extra **mortgage payment** when overtime permits, then consider a shorter roster nearer 2036 if offered.
feel: **Calm** enough to plan, with a dislike of someone else setting the date of my last shift.
S4.quote: I wouldn't trade wages for a vague promise of time off.
fieldNote: She calculates her **age** correctly and sees the decade as a way to retain choice about later shifts.
A shorter roster is **conditional** on cleared debt, workable pension figures and an actual offer; she plans no immediate exit.

steps.text: Keep operator certificate current and request written retirement terms
Make extra mortgage payment when overtime permits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because possible robots around 2031 leave too little time to protect a wage that pays our mortgage. A real purchase timetable and a paid, proven route into other mine work would help, along with honest notice before shifts are cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when a plan on a screen and a worker at the face disagree. I want the worker's safety call recorded and heard before traffic moves.

headlineQuote: I want the worker's safety call recorded and heard before traffic moves.
portrait: **Carla**, 43, operates a shovel at a large mine; her vocational certificate and higher pay help support two children and a mortgage.
She has over **eight months** of savings and nearby mines, yet prefers familiar methods and never uses AI tools.
Under the mild pictures she keeps her **paper handover** and asks for route changes to pass through the site safety meeting.
The **2028** picture worries her most because possible robot shifts arrive around 2031, before she can comfortably replace her wage.
With longer warning she pays down the **mortgage** and checks written retirement terms, without assuming a course or shorter roster exists.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her too little time before possible robot shovels threaten the wage that covers the family mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A real **purchase timetable** and a paid, proven route into other mine work would make decisions possible before shifts are cut.
